PRESIDING JUDGE:

THE HONOURABLE

JACQUES A. NADEAU, J.C.Q.

______________________________________________________________________

THE DIRECTOR OF YOUTH
PROTECTION A,

Director

and

X

(
born on [...], 2002
)

Y

(born on [...], 2000)

Z

(born on [...], 1998)

A

Children

and

Mother

and

Father

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT ON MOTIONS FOR
PROTECTION

(SECTION 38 OF THE
YOUTH
PROTECTION ACT
)

______________________________________________________________________

WARNING :
The
Youth Protection Act
prohibits the
publication or broadcasting of any information that may lead to the
identification of a child or of his parents. Any person who contravenes this
provision commits an offence and is liable to a fine (Sections 11.2.1 and 135
of the
Y.P.A.).

[
1
]

1. THE PROCEEDINGS

[
2
]

The Court is seized of
Motions for Protection

filed pursuant to Section 38 of the
Youth Protection Act
by a person
duly mandated by the Director of Youth Protection A (hereafter, "
the
Director
") on August 8, 2012, to have the security and development of
the [A family] children, A, born on [...], 1996, Z, born on [...], 1998, Y,
born on [...], 2000 and X, born on [...], 2002, declared to be in danger.

[
3
]

The family consists of the mother, the father
and their seven daughters, born between 1991 and 2002. In addition to the four
(4) children who are the subject of youth protection involvement, the daughters
also include D, 22 years old, E, 20 years old, and F, 18 years old.

[
4
]

The parents were separated for approximately ten
(10) years and in the summer of 2012, they decided to reconcile. After dating
for a few months, the father was invited to sleepover at the mother's home on a
few occasions at the beginning of August.

[
5
]

Given the length of their parents' separation,
the children were rather distraught by their reconciliation and a number of
incidents involving the father occurred in the family home which led to the
Director becoming involved.

[
6
]

The older siblings have also alleged a history
of conjugal violence and that this turn of events is but another example of the
father continuing to exert control over the mother and the children.

[
7
]

In addition, the older siblings have raised past
incidents of inappropriate discipline imposed on them on the part of the father
and of the paternal grandmother.

[
8
]

The children have reported being afraid of their
father and refusing to return to the care of their mother.

[
9
]

On August 16, 2012, Mr. Justice Denis Asselin
entrusts the children to the care of their eldest sister, Mrs. D. It should be
noted that at the time, F was also included in this Court order, as she had not
yet reached the age of majority. Once this occurred, the Director filed a
Discontinuance
of Proceedings
with respect to F on April 23, 2013.

[
10
]

The Court adds that since the month of August
2012, there have been a number of
Motions for Interim Measures
brought
before the Court, including the following:

➢

On October 26, 2012 the Director's attorney as
well as the children's attorney requests that the children be able to retrieve
their beds as well as their winter coats.

At the end of the hearing on that day, the parents' attorney at the
time informs the Court that the winter coats were already in the children's
possession but that the mother had disposed of the children's beds which had
been provided by
Agence A
because of her move to a smaller apartment.

➢

On October 26, 2012 the children's lawyer also
requests that F and A be allowed to sleepover nights at a friend's or at their
sister's house with the permission of their eldest sister D. This request is
denied by Mr. Justice Jacques Roy.

➢

In addition, on October 26, 2012 the Director
asks the Court to authorize D to obtain counselling services from
Agence A

for the two (2) youngest children, Y and X. Despite the mother's objection
based on
Agence A's
refusal of the girls returning to her care, the
Court grants the Director's request, recommending that the Director provide
such services, if possible, failing which
Agence A
shall provide them.

➢

On November 13, 2012 the Court has to deal with
a verbal request made by the children's lawyer to authorize the children to
participate in a school activity to be held that week. Mr. Justice Roy allows
the children to participate in this event, including a sleepover, providing
that the activity and sleepover are supervised by their school's principal.

➢

On December 17, 2012 the Court deals with the
father's
Motion
to have the children entrusted to their mother.

Mr. Justice Roy dismisses the father's
Motion
expressing that
he is not sitting on appeal of Mr. Justice Asselin's ruling of August 16th.

Mr. Justice Roy also announces he can no longer continue to preside
the hearings of the
Motions for Protection
because of his limited
availability.

By a judgment rendered on January 9, 2013, Chief Judge Élizabeth
Corte appoints the undersigned to continue the hearing of these
Motions
.

➢

On January 30, 2013 Mr. Justice Louis Grégoire
grants a
Motion
filed by the Director on behalf of F, A and Z,
authorizing them to attend a school activity in New York, as well as a wedding.
He also withdraws the exercise of parental authority relating to school and
normal social activities, conferring this exercise to the Director until the
hearing of the
Motions for Protection.

➢

On April 23, 2013 the Court is requested to make
a number of interim rulings until the hearing resumes on August 6
th
.
In particular, the Court orders the following:

▪

WITHDRAWS
the
attribute of parental authority concerning all documentation relating to
registration for school and school activities from the parents;

▪

CONFERS
this
attribute to the eldest sister of the children, Mrs. D;

▪

WITHDRAWS
the
attribute of parental authority relating to registration for either Camp A or
Camp B from the parents;

▪

CONFERS
this
attribute to the eldest sister of the children, Mrs. D , specifically for
registration of one or several of the children to these two (2) summer camps in
particular;

▪

TAKES JUDICIAL NOTICE
of the Director of Youth Protection's undertaking to allow contacts
between the children and their parents in accordance with the desires and
wishes expressed by the children; and in such a case,

▪

ORDERS
that the
frequency and modalities of contacts between the children and the parents be
determined by the Director of Youth Protection including supervision, if deemed
necessary;

▪

TAKES JUDICIAL NOTICE
of the parents' consent to allow sleepovers requested by the
children at their sister E's home, and in such a case, so long as no males are
present in her apartment for such sleepovers, as well as sleepovers with the
following families: the G family, the H family, the I family and at the home of
J.

➢

On June 14, 2013 the attorney for the children
files a
Motion for Provisional Measures
on behalf of Z, requesting that
she be authorized to attend Camp C for the summer, from June 27th to July 21,
2013.

This
Motion
is contested by the parents and the hearing
begins on June 19
th
and is postponed to July 5
th
to allow
for the testimony of two other (2) witnesses, namely Mrs. K of
Agence A

and Rabbi A, Principal of
A Academy
.

The Court grants the
Motion
and issues the following orders :

▪

AUTHORIZES
Z to
attend Girl Zone Camp in the [Region A] of New York State from Wednesday, July
24th to Tuesday, August 27, 2013;

▪

TAKES JUDICIAL NOTICE
of Rabbi A's undertaking to ensure that a responsible adult be
involved to ensure the appropriate transit of Z to the
Girl Zone Camp

bus in New York City upon her arrival there as well as upon her return;

▪

TAKES JUDICIAL NOTICE
of the mother's offer to accompany Z should Z have a change of heart
and accept that her mother travel with her to and from New York in the context
of her attending Girl Zone Camp;

➢

On August 6, 2013 at the end of the hearing that
day, the children's attorney requests authorization for the children to travel
with their eldest sister D to New York State on August 11
th
to visit
their sister Z at
Girl Zone Camp
. This authorization is denied by the
Court.

➢

Finally, on August 20, 2013, the mother's
attorney files
Motions
in the files of Y and X, alleging certain facts
which allegedly occurred on August 11
th
as well as other facts which
have been raised during the hearing of the
Motions for Protection
.

These
Motions
are scheduled to be presented on September 16
th

when the hearing of the
Motions for Protection
is supposed to conclude.

On September 16
th
, the Court first points out that the
key criteria regarding such a
Motion
is necessity. The Court also refers
to its duty to hear all of the evidence before reaching a decision set out
under Article 77 of the
Youth Protection Act,
which has been interpreted
as conferring considerable powers to the Court in terms of the administration
of proof.

The Court goes on to note that several of the facts alleged in
support of the
Motions
have already been submitted by various witnesses.

[
11
]

In addition to the four days of hearing before
Mr. Justice Jacques Roy in the Fall of 2012, the undersigned had, by September
16
th
, presided an additional four (4) days regarding the
Motions
for Protection
. This does not include the Court time spent in dealing with
some of the other various interim
Motions
referred to above dealing with
issues of travel of certain of the children for a
Sabatton
and a summer
camp in New York.

[
12
]

The hearing date of September 16
th

was scheduled so that the Court could hear the parties' closing arguments, all
of the parties having submitted their evidence.

[
13
]

The Court thus rules that it has sufficient
evidence to make an appropriate ruling as to whether the security and
development of the children are in danger and if so, what measures should be
ordered.

[
14
]

As a result, the Court finds that the
Motions

are not receivable for the following reasons:

1.

They were filed on August 20
th
and
were presentable on September 16
th
, which does not meet the criteria
of urgency and necessity usually associated with this type of
Motion
.

2.

On December 17, 2012, as well as on July 5
th

and on August 6
th
, 2013 the Court was asked to rule on interim
measures which go to the core of its «
enquête
» on the
Motions for
Protection,
namely whether the children's security and development are in
danger and if so, whom should they be entrusted to.

[
15
]

The Court holds that allowing additional
evidence to be submitted at this stage of the proceedings is inappropriate and
contravenes the spirit of the
Youth Protection Act
. It refers to its
inherent power set out under Article 77 of the
Act
. The facts which
occurred on August 11
th
are not of sufficient probative weight in
light of all of the evidence already submitted to the Court to warrant
additional Court time or delays. The
Motions
are thus dismissed.

[
16
]

2. SUMMARY OF THE EVIDENCE

[
17
]

2.1 Evidence of the Director

[
18
]

In addition to the documentary evidence filed in
the Court record, the Director has the following witnesses testify.

[
19
]

2.1.1 Testimony of F

[
20
]

She is seventeen years old when she testifies
and states that she was 6 or 7 when her parents separated.

[
21
]

She kept seeing her father for the weekend
Shabbat

for 4 or 5 years but visits stopped because they were not working out and she
did not feel safe going to see him at the paternal grandmother's house.

[
22
]

F was also confused because her father would say
a lot of bad things about her mother and refer to the arguments they had and
dishes they threw at each other.

[
23
]

Her father came to the mother's home a few times
for visitation with her sisters Y and X.

[
24
]

F remembers her father tying her up with long
ropes once or twice a month due to small things he would get very mad about and
her mother wasn't able to protect her because she was afraid of him. Her
grandmother would help to pull and tighten the ropes as she was living with
them then. The ropes would leave marks on her. She was about 7 or 8 years old
when this happened.

[
25
]

She also remembers her mother being hit by her
father and having bruises, and her and her sisters hiding in another room as
they were afraid to be hit by their father.

[
26
]

The father also spoke disrespectfully to the
mother and told her to shut up.

[
27
]

F recalls the refrigerators being locked by the
grandmother so the mother could not get food on her own.

[
28
]

She describes the atmosphere in the home after
the parents separated as being more calm, normal and stable, with her mother
expressing her opinions.

[
29
]

When the father came back into their life in the
summer of 2012, the mother would not answer her cell phone and would come back
home and would start acting like her father. Her mother's attitude changed and
started being colder like her father whereas she had always been caring and
sensitive.

[
30
]

F testifies that she was shocked at first when
her mother told her she was seeing her father, stating that they were fighting
for the
Guett
for the mother for so many years and it was 2 weeks before
the court date. She adds that they went to many rabbis and a lot of people to
support them, and that her and her sisters were all ready to testify in
Superior Court for what the father had done to them in the past. She states
that the mother fell into the father's trap.

[
31
]

She felt a mix of emotions, describing herself
as mad, angry and confused.

[
32
]

F recalls one night when the mother was at a
hotel and the children were left alone without any supervision. She says they
were scared and that she tried to call her mother many times on her cell phone
and she wasn't answering. She was very worried for her.

[
33
]

In a span of 1 to 2 weeks, she mentions that the
father started coming to their house, staying over for the whole day with the
mother. She was not comfortable with that and told her mother a few times but
she did not listen to her.

[
34
]

F describes an incident when her younger sister Z
wanted to watch television and the father told her to turn it off which she
refused to do. The father then took her by the hand, squeezed it tightly and
twisted it while telling her to close the television. She denies that Z tried
to hit the father. The mother then did the same thing, squishing Z's wrist. She
claims Z had a mark.

[
35
]

Y and X were in bed in their room, heard what
was going on and started crying.

[
36
]

Z then left the house with A and F claims that
the father locked the front and back doors so they would not be able to enter
the house

upon their return.

[
37
]

She states that every time she would try to give
her opinion, the father would put her down and tell her if she did not agree,
she could leave the house and that he would find her a foster home. Her mother
would copy him.

[
38
]

F claims that the father took out the
Internet
,
the television as well as her sister's phone while impersonating her with her
phone. He also made her and her sisters dress more conservatively. He claimed
they were misbehaving.

[
39
]

He imposed a lot of rules in a very short time
and the children were not even comfortable with him being there. He did not
apologize for what he did to them in the past and it was an awkward relationship
with them.

[
40
]

Their mother did not voice her opinions any more
and if she would try to intervene, the father would put his hand close to her
mouth and tell her to be quiet.

[
41
]

While E was away for a vacation, the father
turned her room into a storage area.

[
42
]

Since their entrustment to their eldest sister D,
she had a few visits with her mother, once at their school and the other ones
with all of her sisters at the Director's offices as well as at her mother's
house. She found the first to be embarrassing as it was in front of all of her
friends. As for the other visits, the children spoke to the mother and it
didn't really go well because everybody was really angry at her. F was very
disappointed with her mother's answers.

[
43
]

She refuses to go back home because she doesn't
trust her mother who lied to her about seeing her father. She states that
therapy for every member of the family would be required for the children to go
back home.

[
44
]

As for contacts, she mentions she would like
weekly supervised contacts with her mother but is not comfortable to have
contacts with her father yet.

[
45
]

F is receiving individual therapy from
Auberge
A
as well as tutoring from
[Agence A]
.

[
46
]

On cross-examination, she explains that at D's
in Ville A, there are two separate apartments across the hall from one another
on the fourth floor and that the doors are open all the time during the day and
locked at night. In the younger girls' apartment, there is a master bedroom in
which A and Z sleep in a queen-size bed while she sleeps on the individual bed,
whereas in the room right next door, Y and X sleep on a queen-size bed. D's
husband is the janitor for the building.

[
47
]

D and her husband have a year and a half old
child. The girls go to school during the day and when they return to the
apartment, they have a meal together in their apartment which has a dining
room. D is there when they do their homework and prepare for bed. F is in
charge of locking the door around 10 P.M. and has a phone on her in case.

[
48
]

Only A and her have the keys, as they are mostly
in charge of their apartment.

[
49
]

In the morning, the girls wake up at 6 A.M.,
unlock the door, prepare their snacks and lunches and leave for school under D's
supervision.

[
50
]

They have to be in the apartment by 8 P.M. and
sleepovers at their friends' home are not allowed by their parents.

[
51
]

2.1.2 Testimony of Z

[
52
]

She is fourteen years old when she testifies.
She was about five 5 years old when her parents separated. She had contacts
with her father until she was eleven years old and then they had a fight on the
telephone and stopped seeing each other.

[
53
]

Z used to celebrate
Shabbat
at her
father's house every weekend with either Y or X. She always felt controlled by
him because he always put rules on her and she never really liked it. He would
call her at her mother's home and she would have to answer him and tell him she
was obeying those rules, even as a child.

[
54
]

There were not as many rules at her mother's
home but the children all knew their limits.

[
55
]

She states that she did not accept her mother
reconciling with her father and questioned her as to why she was doing so. She
replied that their father had changed but when he came to the mother's home, Z
says that he was exactly the same, as he was abusive and controlling (putting
rules). He did not apologize to her nor to her sisters. He would ask for things
such as a cup of water and she felt he looked at her with the requirement of
her having to respect him.

[
56
]

She declares that her father started coming over
and bringing things like food to the mother. He was treating her like nothing,
like he didn't even care about her. When the girls and the father argued a bit
and the mother tried to interfere, he would tell her to be quiet.

[
57
]

According to Z, before her father's return, she
had a close relationship with her mother whom she referred to as an amazing
mum. Upon his return, she didn't act like herself any more, she acted like him.
She would only speak when she had something of his to say.

[
58
]

She refers to new rules in the home, such as
wearing pants instead of shorts as pyjamas, taking away the
Internet
and
establishing a bedtime in the summer. He would bring fresh croissants and
baguettes in the morning but tell some of the children to get their own bread
from the freezer because they were not obeying his rules.

[
59
]

Z refers to the incident when she was watching
television with her mother in the evening to get their mind off the day of fast
they were going through. The father came and said they were not to watch
television and the mother agreed. When they were about to pull the plug of the
television out, Z disagreed and said it was unfair. Her father took her by her
wrist and twisted her arm with all his force, and held it up high which hurt
her and made her cry. She asked him to stop, his face was all red and he looked
mad. The mother asked him to stop. When Z continued preventing them from taking
the plug out, her mother started twisting her arm like her father, but she
managed to push her away. The other children were in the home when this
happened and they were afraid. Y and X were crying, and A and Z had to comfort
them.

[
60
]

After this altercation, Z left the home with A.
She was stressed, frustrated and mad, and her sister was calming her down. When
they returned around 2 or 3 A.M., the front door was locked. The back door,
which was always open, was also locked. They managed to enter the home and saw
the father who got out of bed and asked them how they got into the house.

[
61
]

Afterwards, she did not speak to either of her
parents because she was mad at both of them. She felt that there was no use of
speaking to her mother.

[
62
]

Z also recounts an incident which occurred at
the synagogue when she was 4 or 5 and had cried to obtain a box of prizes. Her
father asked the paternal grandmother to help him tie her up in ropes outside
of the synagogue and she was put in the trunk of the car before they drove
away. She was not able to move and was screaming and crying.

[
63
]

Z points out that at D's, they sometimes eat in
their apartment, and sometimes in D's apartment. They all eat together as a big
family. They all handle breakfast and making lunches for school independently
while helping their younger sisters out.

[
64
]

A woman from
[Agence A]
comes on
Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays to help them with supper and lunches for
school, as well as laundry and cleaning the apartment.

[
65
]

She is seeing a social worker and is also
attending tutoring programs at
[Agence A]
which has also helped them
with food and clothing.

[
66
]

Z misses what she calls her mother's real self
and only wants to have contacts with her if she goes to therapy. She does not
want any contacts with her father.

[
67
]

On cross-examination, she declares that when the
father came back in July of 2012, he often screamed at the children when they
didn't follow his rules and even told them to shut up on one occasion.

[
68
]

She confirms that she was disappointed and angry
to hear that her mother was not going to move forward on obtaining the
Guett
.

[
69
]

She comments the
document filed as Exhibit M-1, «
Sperm Donor's Chair
»,
which her sister A drafted but put in
her drawer before it was found by the father who took it. She is very sure it
was never put on the father's chair.

[
70
]

2.1.3 Testimony of A

[
71
]

She is 16 years old when she testifies. She was
about 7 years old when her parents separated. She had contacts with her father
for a few years before they got into a fight and stopped talking for 5 years
straight.

[
72
]

Contacts would take place at her grandmother's
house and would always involve F and herself. They were day visits and involved
normal activities such as grocery shopping.

[
73
]

She called her father up one day and told him
she no longer wanted to speak to him because of he was very controlling and
pressuring her. He would say that the mother was not responsible and speak
badly about her. She was very angry and frustrated because she was confused.

[
74
]

A states that the whole family went to Court to
help the mother obtain the
Guett
to support her and testify in her
favour. The importance of this for the mother was to acquire her independence
and obtain her freedom from the father's controlling ways. The parents were
usually fighting and it was not a pleasant thing. Her grandmother used to hit
her on her arm at the request of her father.

[
75
]

She saw her father tie her sister Z up with a
rope.

[
76
]

After her parents separated, her mother, D and E
provided help with discipline.

[
77
]

She explains that before her parents'
reconciliation, her mother was a caring and generous person but when the father
came back, she totally changed, forgot about the children and put the father in
front of them.

[
78
]

A says she gave the father a chance but
witnessed the arm twisting incident involving Z which really scared her.

[
79
]

Z was screaming and telling him to let go, which
he did when the mother intervened. He was all red and frustrated. All of a
sudden, the mother took Z's arm again to do the exact same thing while Z was
asking her why she was doing that.

[
80
]

A confirms that she and Z went out for a walk
afterwards because they were very frustrated and needed to get their minds off
everything. Upon their return, the front door was locked and to their surprise,
so was the back door. After they managed to get inside the house, the father
got up and asked them what they were doing there. They replied by asking him
where did he expect them to go. Both A and Z felt really hurt by this incident.

[
81
]

She claims there were a lot of fights and
disagreements at home and that the father was just trying to gain control
again.

[
82
]

She refers to asking for a piece of fresh baguette
one morning and the father intervening to deny her request and telling her to
get her own bread from the freezer. She also states that the father would tell
her to go to her room and to go to bed at 11 P.M.

[
83
]

She does not wish to see her mother as she feels
she is like her father and is not the same person any more.

[
84
]

School has been very supporting for her and she
is receiving social services from an
[Agence A]
social worker.

[
85
]

At D's, there is a chart identifying everyone's
tasks. F and herself are usually there to watch over the younger children, as
well as D and her husband.

[
86
]

As for Exhibit M-1, she wrote it and was going
to put it on her father's chair but her sister told her not do so and she thus
put it back in her drawer and closed it. She says what she wrote is what she
feels because the father was never there for them and there was never a normal
relationship between him and her.

[
87
]

Upon her father's return, he also told A to stop
seeing and sleeping over at her best friend's house. He also took away her
phone because she was not going to bed at 11 P.M. Her father then used her
phone to impersonate her by texting some of her friends.

[
88
]

She is undecided as to whether she wants to see
her mother or not. She would rather stay with her sisters than with friends
because she knows the family will be there forever.

[
89
]

2.1.4 Testimony of E

[
90
]

She is nineteen years old when she testifies.
She left the mother's home when she returned from Israel during the Summer of
2012. Her mother no longer wanted to talk to her because of a letter she wrote
to
[Agence A]
about what was happening in her mother's home. Her mother
had told her she did not want her to come home when she was in Israel.

[
91
]

E claims to have been emotionally abused by her
father when she was younger.

[
92
]

He was very, very strict and would slap her on
the butt to discipline her. She recalls the fear of him hitting her.

[
93
]

She saw her parents get into an argument and the
father poking the mother with a curtain rod in the kitchen and her mother
throwing a glass on the floor.

[
94
]

After her parents' separation when she was about
nine (9) or ten (10), she saw her father on alternate weekends for one (1) or
two (2) years. They got into a fight about her going to a religious play with
her family on a school night and they stopped speaking for several years.

[
95
]

When they started seeing each other again, he
offered to tutor her but requested that in exchange, she tell the mother that
he be allowed to come in the house.

5.1 The relevant burden of proof

[
339
]

Since these proceedings are of a civil nature,
the Director must establish the facts giving rise to the applicable legal
presumption in accordance with the criterion of the preponderance of evidence,
as set out under
Article 2804
of the
Civil Code of Québec
, which states
that:

Evidence is
sufficient if it renders the existence of a fact more probable than its
non-existence, unless the law requires more convincing proof.

[
340
]

For some time, certain rulings applied a
standard of proof of a higher degree when criminal or morally reprehensible
behaviour was involved.

[
341
]

However, in the Supreme Court ruling of
F. H. McDougall
,
2008 SCC 53 (CanLII)
, 2008
C.S.C. 53,

Mr. Justice Marshall Rothstein concluded that there is but one standard of
proof in civil matters, namely that of the balance of probabilities:

[40] Like the House of Lords, I think it is
time to say, once and for all in Canada, that there is only one civil standard
of proof at common law and that is proof on a balance of probabilities.
Of course, context is all important and a judge should not be unmindful, where
appropriate, of inherent probabilities or improbabilities or the seriousness of
the allegations or consequences.  However, these considerations do not
change the standard of proof.  I am of the respectful opinion that the
alternatives I have listed above should be rejected for the reasons that
follow.

[…]

[49] In the result, I would reaffirm that
in
civil cases there is only one standard of proof and that is proof on a balance
of probabilities
.  In all civil cases, the trial judge must scrutinize
the relevant evidence with care to determine
whether it is more likely than
not that an alleged event occurred.

(our emphasis)

[
342
]

It is in light of these principles that the Court must now rule on
the issues at hand.

[

The Court adds that the continuous stream of

set out at the beginning of this judgment, the incidents relating to the

[
422
]

The Court finds that the case of these children
is clearly distinguishable from that of the adolescents involved in the
judgment cited by the father's attorney, X – and – Y – and – A – and – B
[1]
, rendered by Mr. Justice Michel Dubois, if only because of the
number of years of the parents' separation in the case at hand, during which

[
423
]

In a judgment rendered by Mr. Justice Omer Boudreau on April 18,
1997
[2]
, the Court sets out a number of criteria to be considered before
declaring that the security or development of a child is endangered in this
type of situation:

La Loi sur la protection de la jeunesse ne peut
concerner tous les cas où un enfant est affecté pour une courte période de
temps ou raison de la séparation de ses parents. Avant de déclarer compromis la
sécurité et ou développement d'un enfant concerné par ce genre de situation,
les critères suivants apparaissent devoir être considérés :

1)

La
période de temps pendant laquelle l'enfant est affecté par cette situation;

2)

La nature
et l'intensité du conflit entre les parents impliqués;

3)

Les
attitudes et les comportements des deux parents l'un à l'égard de l'autre en
présence de l'enfant;

4)

L'utilisation
des enfants comme «outils» et instrument de négociation des parents, l'un à
l'égard de l'autre et l'effet de ce comportement sur l'enfant.

(at pages 2 and 3 – our emphasis)

[
424
]

The Court finds that when these criteria are applied to the case at
hand, a declaration of endangerment clearly is warranted in these
circumstances.

[
425
]

In reaching this conclusion, the Court is not only mindful, but also
respectful, of the religious beliefs of not only the parents but of the
children as well.

[
426
]

In a judgment of January 11, 1990
[3]
the
Court was seized of a matter in which the parents were Jehovah witnesses and
had two children of 16 and 14 years of age. The children where seeking foster
home placement until they reached the age of majority because they did not wish
to practice their parents' religion. Mr. Justice Constant Cordeau first noted
that each of the facts alleged, taken individually, could not constitute a
ground of endangerment, but when all of the requirements and prohibitions of
this religion, as well as their impacts on the children are taken as a whole,
such a finding was warranted.

[
427
]

Mr. Justice Cordeau states the following regarding freedom of
religion:

Le Tribunal doit tout d'abord dire que les parents ont
le droit de pratiquer la religion de leur choix et la pratique d'une religion
ne constitue certainement pas un motif de compromission énuméré à l'article 38
de la Loi sur la protection de la jeunesse tout comme le Tribunal doit dire que
la pratique d'une religion ou l'adhésion aux principes d'une religion ne
saurait constituer un motif acceptable pour que les parents transgressent les
motifs énumérés à l'article 38 de la Loi.

Le Tribunal n'a pas à porter de jugement de valeur sur
une religion plutôt que sur une autre. Le Tribunal doit regarder la situation
selon les principes de droit actuellement en vigueur.

(at page 16 – our emphasis)

[
428
]

The Court then goes on to cite
Article 3
of the

Québec
Charter of Human Rights

and Freedoms
which provides that:

Every person is the possessor of the
fundamental freedoms, including freedom of conscience, freedom of religion,
freedom of opinion, freedom of expression, freedom of peaceful assembly and
freedom of association.

[
429
]

Mr. Justice Cordeau finds that these fundamental
rights apply both to the parents and their children:

Le Tribunal doit constater que cet
article 3
stipulant
toute personne s'applique autant aux enfants âgés de seize ans et quatorze ans
et demi qu'à leurs parents.

C'est dire que ces enfants eux aussi sont titulaires
de libertés fondamentales et ont
le droit à la liberté de conscience, la
liberté de religion et la liberté d'opinion
.

D'autre part, les parents assoient leurs croyances et
aussi leurs convictions bien sûr sur leurs principes religieux, mais aussi sur
leur conception de leur autorité parentale qu'ils semblent considérer comme un
droit absolu, ne supportant aucune contestation.

(at pages 17 and 18 – our emphasis)

[
430
]

The notion of parental authority is dealt with
in
Articles 597
to
612
of the
Civil Code of Québec
. As Mr. Justice
Cordeau points out, this right is not absolute and one or either of the parents
may be deprived of such authority by the Court for a serious reason and in the
interest of the child.

[
431
]

Both Article 33 of the
Civil Code
and
Article 3 of the
Youth Protection Act
emphasize that every decision
concerning a child shall be taken in light of the child's interests and the
respect of his rights.

[
432
]

Moreover, in addition to the moral,
intellectual, emotional and material needs of the child, his age, health,
personality and family environment and the other aspects of the situation must
be taken into account.

[
433
]

Mr. Justice Cordeau found that the situation
imposed upon the 2 children as established by the evidence did not comply with
their interest or their rights.

[
434
]

The following comments of Mr. Justice Cordeau
are also relevant to the matters at hand:

Ces enfants-là n'ont pas témoigné sous le coup de la
colère ou d'une impulsion passagère; ils ont eu le temps de réfléchir à la
situation et malgré cela ils ne souhaitent toujours pas retourner chez leurs
parents.

De quoi les enfants sont-ils menacés et quels risques
courent-ils? Le Tribunal peut en faire une énumération qui n'est pas
exhaustive.

Tout d'abord, les enfants, à l'âge qu'ils ont, avec la
détermination qui est la leur et l'intelligence brillante qu'ils démontrent,
seront parfaitement capables de faire ce qu'il faut pour se faire sortir de
leur famille, que ce soit pas des problèmes de comportement ou autrement
et le garçon le plus vieux a déjà montré
des signes en s'enfuyant la nuit de chez eux pour aller traîner sur la rue
jusqu'aux petites heures du matin.

[…]

Enfin, un dernier risque moral et affectif que
risquent les enfants et le Tribunal est surpris que les parents ne l'aient pas
déjà réalisé,
c'est
le risque que ces enfants se détachent de leurs parents et que cela se fasse en
douceur ou en silence ou bien que cela se fasse dans l'agressivité, le dommage
en sera aussi grand pour les enfants.
Et ce sont là toutes des situations facilement
prévisibles, à cause de l'ensemble de la situation dans laquelle se trouvent
les enfants, qui menace leur développement mental ou affectif et qui risque de
leur créer un danger moral.

(at pages 23 and 24 – our emphasis)

[
435
]

The Court concludes that the same risks exist in
this family and hopes that it is not too late to reverse the current trend. The
history of the parents' separation over a period of ten years, coupled with
their unforeseeable reconciliation in the Summer of 2012 and the legal battle
in Court over the past year, has created a poisoned family environment.

[
436
]

A good example of this is the document filed as
Exhibit M-1, drafted by A, containing the words «
Sperm Donor's Chair
».
In her testimony, A says that what she wrote is what she feels because the
father was never there for her and her sisters and that there was never a
normal relationship between the both of them. She adds that she was going to
put it on her father's chair but Z told her not to. She thus put it back in her
drawer and closed it.

[
437
]

Although the Court does not endorse the use of
such words, they nevertheless reflect a feeling of betrayal on the part of A.

[
438
]

For all of these reasons, the parents' repeated
conduct has caused emotional harm to the children and the parents have failed
to take the necessary steps to put an end to the situation. As a result, the Court
rules that they have been subjected to psychological ill-treatment pursuant to
Subsection 38 c) of the
Youth Protection Act
.

[
439
]

5.9 The appropriate measures

[
440
]

The living arrangements
described at D's home, although not ideal, are perfectly suitable in light of
the circumstances.

[
441
]

The Court notes that
Agence A
is
providing help to D with the support of a worker. Moreover, the girls have
adapted relatively well and comply with the rules set out by D, including
curfews and a chore list.

[
442
]

This being said, the Court finds that this is
not a permanent solution and this is why the situation will need to be reviewed
at the end of August 2014.

[
443
]

Clearly, the parents need to put an end to the
escalation they have engaged in over the past year and a half if they wish to
reconnect with the children in the months to come. The Court strongly
encourages them to have a more cooperative attitude when dealing with the
social workers involved in the family situation.

[
444
]

The issue of therapy was raised at the hearing
and remains relevant as a first step towards acknowledging what the children
have been subjected to.

[
445
]

Given the parents' acrimony towards D and her
husband, the Court rules that certain attributes of parental authority
regarding authorizations or consents relating to health or medical care and
services, school and extracurricular activities, social activities, passports
and travelling should be withdrawn from the parents and conferred to D for the
time being.

[
446
]

At the hearing, the parents also voiced their
disapproval of social worker [Social Worker 1]'s handling of the family
situation. The Court finds that in these trying circumstances, Mrs. [Social
Worker 1] acted to the best of her abilities but will nevertheless recommend
that a new social worker be assigned to these matters to attempt to get things
back on track.

[
447
]

In closing, the Court invites both the parents are the children to
seriously reflect on the choice which they will have to make as a result of
this judgment: either make the gap between themselves wider or on the other
hand, begin building bridges to restore the relations between them, in which
case the Court deems therapy to be advisable.

[
448
]

6. CONCLUSIONS

449

into consideration the various documents filed in the Court record as well as

Youth Protection Act
